title: When the Sahara Was Green
yt_title: When the Sahara Was Green: Hippos, Lakes and a Lost Lineage
verdict_scope: A green Sahara, with lakes, hippos, crocodiles, fishers and herders, from about 14,500 to 5,000 years ago, paced by the slow wobble of Earth's orbit through the West African monsoon: Established (lake shorelines, fossils, pollen, dust and leaf-wax records, and the archaeology of hundreds of sites). Graded separately in the weighing: the orbit and the monsoon as its pacemaker: Established (how much the vegetation feedback added is still debated); a North African lineage nobody knew, from the Takarkori genomes: Strong evidence (two women, one site); Nabta Playa's ring watching the sun: Plausible (the star maps: a stretch); the Sahara switching off overnight: Mixed record (abrupt in some records, gradual in others, later further south); Gobero one people or two, the meaning of the swimmers, and drought as the spark of Egypt: Open question; the Garamantes undone by their fossil water: Plausible; astronauts on the rocks: Ruled out.
hook: How did the Sahara turn green?
end_line: Somewhere under the sand, the green Sahara is still waiting to be read.

shots.say: In the southern Sahara, in what is now Chad, there was once a lake as big as the Caspian Sea. That's the largest lake on Earth today. Geologists call it Lake Mega-Chad.
shots.draw: A map of the Chad basin (about 6 to 26 E, 6 to 24 N) with the national borders faint: today's Lake Chad, a small blue patch; then Lake Mega-Chad fills outward from it (a schematic outline scaled to about 360,000 square km), deep blue. On 'the Caspian Sea' the outline of the Caspian, drawn to the same scale, slides in beside it as a dashed blue shape: about the same size. shots.say: Its old beaches still ring the desert, clear enough to trace from space.
shots.draw: Seen from orbit: a satellite in the top right sends a pale scanning beam down onto a sand plain; old shorelines draw themselves one after another as long concentric curved ridges in the sand, a ring of beach ridges around a dry basin; a tiny camel and rider for scale. shots.say: And across the Sahara, dried-up lake beds hold the bones of fish, hippos and crocodiles: animals that need water all year round.
shots.draw: A dried lake bed cut open: pale lake mud layers under the sand. As named, fossils pop in the layers: a fish skeleton, a hippo jaw with its tusks, a crocodile jaw with teeth; above each, the living animal appears as a faint dashed outline swimming in a ghost of the old water line. Label 'old lake beds'.

shots.say: But why? Earth's orbit has a slow wobble, about twenty thousand years long, that changes which season we spend closest to the Sun. Ten thousand years ago, that was the northern summer. Summer sunshine over North Africa was about seven percent stronger.
shots.draw: Space: the Sun at the left, Earth's orbit as an ellipse (shape exaggerated) with the closest point marked; a curved arrow runs along the orbit, 'about 20,000 years': the season at the closest point slowly changes. At the closest point, a dashed Earth 'today: January' tilted away, then a solid Earth '10,000 years ago: northern summer' with the north tilted towards the Sun and North Africa lit. shots.draw: A loop drawn as a landscape: on the left bright bare sand bounces the sunlight back up (yellow arrows reflected); on the right grass, trees and a pond darken the ground and take the light in; wavy vapour rises from the plants and the water into a growing cloud, the cloud rains back on the plants, and a circular arrow closes around them: 'more plants, more rain'.

shots.say: A few crocodiles still live in rock pools in the desert of Mauritania. They're survivors of the green Sahara.
shots.draw: Dusk in a rocky desert canyon: a small dark rock pool (a guelta) at the foot of the cliffs, a crocodile basking on a ledge at the water's edge, its reflection in the pool; sand all around. A small locator map in the corner with a pin in Mauritania. Label 'a guelta, Mauritania'.

shots.say: In the year 2000, dinosaur hunters in Niger's Ténéré desert found human bones in the sand. The team was led by the palaeontologist Paul Sereno.
shots.draw: Rolling dunes in hard light; a field team on the crest (three figures, one kneeling with a brush beside a huge dinosaur leg bone half out of the sand). Nearby a few small pale bone fragments show in the sand beside a little marker flag. Inset map: Niger with a pin 'Gobero', the Air Mountains and the Tenere marked. Labels 'Gobero, Niger, 2000'.

shots.say: It was a cemetery: about two hundred graves, on a dune beside a lake that has since vanished. The lake was about three kilometres across, and no more than three metres deep.
shots.draw: Plan view: a long sand ridge on which about two hundred small oval graves pop one by one; beside it the outline of the vanished lake fills blue, with a '3 km' bar across it. Then a small section of the lake below: a shallow water layer and a standing person for scale, '3 m' at its deepest.

shots.say: In the rubbish heaps: bones of Nile perch, catfish and hippos, and harpoons and fish hooks made of bone.
shots.draw: A low midden heap in section, shells and ash; out of it rise, one by one as named, a big Nile perch, a whiskered catfish, a hippo (side view); then two bone harpoon points with barbs and a bone fish hook, drawn large and pale like museum pieces. Labels 'Nile perch', 'catfish', 'hippo', 'bone harpoons'.

shots.say: The first people buried here are called the Kiffian. From about 7700 BCE, they fished the lake with harpoons. Then came a long dry spell, and the lake emptied. For about a thousand years, no one was buried here.
shots.draw: A time line from 8000 to 2000 BCE under a lake drawn as a water level: from 7700 BCE the lake fills (blue), a fisher with a harpoon stands at its edge and small grave marks appear, 'Kiffian'; from 6200 BCE the water drains away to cracked mud, 'dry'; a bracket over 6200 to 5200 BCE: 'about 1,000 years', no graves.
shots.reuse: gobero (16.06) mural shot 4: the lake that fills, empties and fills again

shots.say: When the water came back, so did the burials, but they looked different. These people are called the Tenerians, and they also kept cattle.
shots.draw: Same time line: from 5200 BCE the lake fills again; new grave marks in another colour, a herder with cattle at the shore; label 'Tenerian'.

shots.say: About fifty-three hundred years ago, a woman and two children were laid in one grave, their arms and legs intertwined. Clumps of pollen from wild flowers suggest flowers were laid with them.
shots.draw: No remains are drawn: a grave outline in the sand seen from above, and inside it three soft lights of different sizes close together (a woman and two children), their glows overlapping. shots.draw: Left a group of three figures in blue ('Kiffian'), right three in gold ('Tenerian'), a wall line between them tagged '2008: two peoples'. Then a molar seen from above, its cusps ringed one by one. Then a row of teeth from each group lines up and an '≈' glows between them: 'newer study: alike'; the wall line fades to dashes.

shots.say: One people, or two? Ancient DNA could settle it, if any survived the heat. Either way, someone loved them.
shots.draw: Back at the three lights of the embrace (the panel of s20): a dashed double helix with a question mark hovers over the grave; a hot sun glows at the top; then the three lights brighten warmly, the flowers around them.

shots.say: In 2002, a second shelter turned up about ten kilometres away: the Cave of Beasts. Its painted wall is about seventeen metres long. About eight thousand figures. And about eight thousand years old.
shots.draw: A long low shelter: an overhanging lip of rock over a wide pale wall; a 'about 17 m' dimension line draws under it, with three standing people for scale; then thousands of tiny painted marks (red, white, ochre) spread over the wall; labels pop: 'about 8,000 figures', then 'about 8,000 years old'.
shots.reuse: wadi-sura (16.07) mural shot 2: the wall of the Cave of Beasts, redrawn wide

shots.say: Hands, swimmers, and strange headless beasts. A few tiny hand stencils looked like a baby's. Measured against real newborns' hands, they turned out to be most likely the feet of a reptile, perhaps a lizard.
shots.draw: Close on the wall: a hand stencil (a hand outline in a cloud of red spray), a swimmer, and a headless beast pop as named. Then a tiny stencil is ringed; beside it a newborn's hand outline in dashes does not match (a red cross); a lizard's front foot is drawn and matches the stencil (a green tick). Labels 'a baby's hand?', 'a reptile's foot'.
shots.reuse: wadi-sura (16.07) mural shot 3: a stencil and a lizard's foot

shots.say: In a rock shelter in south-west Libya, two women were laid to rest about seven thousand years ago. The shelter is called Takarkori. Back then, herders lived here with their cattle, beside lakes and grassland.

shots.say: At Nabta Playa, in Egypt's southern desert, cattle herders set up a ring of stones about four metres across. A playa is a dry lake bed that fills only after rain. Back then, summer rains filled it every year, and herders came with their cattle.

Right: a playa in section, a shallow hollow in the desert floor; rain streaks fall, the hollow fills with a seasonal lake, and herders and cattle arrive at its edge.

shots.say: Slowly, as Earth's orbit turned, the monsoon that had greened the Sahara retreated south. So did the green Sahara switch off overnight?

shots.say: Off the coast of Mauritania, the dust blown out to sea jumps about five and a half thousand years ago, within decades to centuries. But a lake in Chad called Yoa tells a slower story: its trees thin out over thousands of years.
shots.draw: A small map strip at the top with pins 'off Mauritania' and 'Lake Yoa, Chad'. Below, a graph from 8,000 to 3,000 years ago, 'wet' at the top and 'dry' at the bottom: a red line drops like a cliff at about 5,500 years ago ('off Mauritania'); then a green line slopes down slowly over thousands of years ('Lake Yoa').

description:
About nine thousand years ago, hippos surfaced in lakes in the middle of what is now the Sahara. For thousands of years, monsoon rains turned the biggest hot desert on Earth green, with a lake in Chad as big as the Caspian Sea. How did it happen, who lived there, and how fast did the rain stop?

We follow the clues: Lake Mega-Chad and the slow wobble of Earth's orbit, the lakeside cemetery of Gobero and its embrace, the painted swimmers of Wadi Sura, the ancient DNA of Takarkori, the stone ring of Nabta Playa, the end of the rains and the move to the Nile and the oases, and the Garamantes, who drank fossil water. A green Sahara: Established. A North African lineage nobody knew: Strong evidence. Nabta watching the sun: Plausible. The switch-off: Mixed record. Astronauts on the rocks: Ruled out.

facts_added.fact: Palaeolake Mega-Chad covered at least 400,000 square km, bigger than the Caspian Sea (the largest lake on Earth today), and was over 173 m deep; its shorelines are mapped from satellite imagery.
facts_added.source: Drake & Bristow 2006, The Holocene, doi:10.1191/0959683606hol981rr

facts_added.fact: Lake Mega-Chad was at its peak by about 11,500 years ago and lasted until about 5,000 years ago, when its level fell rapidly; the Bodele basin dried finally about 1,000 years ago and is today the world's greatest single dust source.
facts_added.source: Armitage, Bristow & Drake 2015, PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.1417655112

facts_added.fact: About 10,000 years ago Earth was closest to the Sun in the northern summer (half a precession cycle ago); summer radiation over North Africa was about 7 percent higher than today; the warmer land draws moist air in from the tropical Atlantic.
facts_added.source: deMenocal & Tierney 2012, Nature Education Knowledge 3(10): 12

facts_added.fact: The African Humid Period ran from about 14,800 to 5,500 years ago (interrupted by the Younger Dryas); off Mauritania its onset and end each took decades to centuries, when summer insolation crossed a threshold about 4.2 percent above today's.
facts_added.source: deMenocal et al. 2000, Quaternary Science Reviews, doi:10.1016/S0277-3791(99)00081-5

facts_added.fact: At its height the Green Sahara received about ten times today's rainfall (leaf-wax records; roughly 250 to 1,670 mm a year against under 100 today).
facts_added.source: Tierney, Pausata & deMenocal 2017, Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.1601503

facts_added.fact: A review finds clear evidence of a Holocene megalake only in the Chad basin; other proposed Saharan megalakes lack it, and a 'pale-green and discontinuously wet Sahara' of wetlands and small lakes fits the evidence better.
facts_added.source: Quade et al. 2018, Quaternary Research, doi:10.1017/qua.2018.46

facts_added.fact: A climate model reproduces an abrupt Saharan desertification in the mid-Holocene: subtle orbital changes strongly amplified by atmosphere-vegetation feedbacks.
facts_added.source: Claussen et al. 1999, Geophysical Research Letters, doi:10.1029/1999GL900494

facts_added.fact: Crocodiles survive in 78 localities in Mauritania, mostly in rocky pools called gueltas: relict populations of the wetter mid-Holocene Sahara.
facts_added.source: Brito et al. 2011, PLoS ONE, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0014734

facts_added.fact: Gobero was found in 2000 during a palaeontological expedition led by Paul Sereno; about 200 burials; the lake was no more than 3 m deep and 3 km across; middens hold Nile perch, large catfish, hippos and crocodiles, with bone harpoon points and hooks.
facts_added.source: Sereno et al. 2008, PLoS ONE, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0002995; Sereno lab, 'People of the Green Sahara'

facts_added.fact: Gobero phases: Kiffian about 7700 to 6200 BCE, abandonment in a dry phase about 6200 to 5200 BCE, Tenerian about 5200 to 2500 BCE with some cattle; the triple burial (an adult woman and two children with intertwined arms and legs) dates to about 3315 BCE, with clusters of wool-flower (Celosia) pollen between the arms and in the sediment beneath.
facts_added.source: Sereno et al. 2008, PLoS ONE, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0002995

facts_added.fact: In 2008 the excavators read the skulls as a population replacement; a dental study (20 Kiffian, 30 Tenerian) finds the two phases dentally indistinguishable, with closest affinities to Nile Valley populations such as al-Khiday in Sudan.
facts_added.source: Stojanowski, Irish & Sereno 2026 (first published online 25 May 2026), American Journal of Biological Anthropology, doi:10.1002/ajpa.70262

facts_added.fact: The Cave of Swimmers was found by Laszlo Almasy in October 1933 on the DIAFE expedition; Almasy read the swimmers as real swimming and evidence of a climate change; Hans Rhotert and later Jean-Loic Le Quellec read them as the dead floating in the primeval waters (Nun).
facts_added.source: Kuper (ed.) 2013, Wadi Sura: The Cave of Beasts; Le Quellec, de Flers & de Flers 2005

facts_added.fact: The Cave of Beasts (Wadi Sura II), found in 2002 about 10 km west of the Cave of Swimmers, has a decorated rear wall about 17 to 18 m wide (sources differ: 17 m in the Wadi Sura project summaries, 18 m in Forster, Riemer & Kuper 2012) and up to 6 m high with about 8,000 figures, including more than 30 headless beasts and hundreds of hand stencils; its art belongs to the Gilf B phase, about 6500 to 4400 cal BC ('about 8,000 years ago' in the monograph).
facts_added.source: Forster, Riemer & Kuper 2012, The Signs of Which Times? (Brussels): 197-216; Kuper (ed.) 2013, Africa Praehistorica 26

facts_added.fact: The tiny 'baby' hand stencils of Wadi Sura II differ in size, proportions and shape from the hands of newborn and premature babies: most probably a reptile's.
facts_added.source: Honore et al. 2016, Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, doi:10.1016/j.jasrep.2016.02.014

facts_added.fact: Saharan rock art depicts cattle herding by early pastoral groups and includes rare scenes of milking; pottery from Takarkori holds the first unequivocal chemical evidence of dairying in Africa, in the fifth millennium BC.
facts_added.source: Dunne et al. 2012, Nature, doi:10.1038/nature11186

facts_added.fact: The Takarkori genomes come from two naturally mummified adult women (about 7,158 to 6,796 and 6,555 to 6,281 calibrated years ago); about 93 percent of their ancestry is an unknown North African lineage, about 7 percent Levantine; it diverged from sub-Saharan lineages about when the ancestors of non-Africans did (put at about 50,000 years ago by the team's institute) and stayed isolated; their closest known relatives are the 15,000-year-old foragers of Taforalt, Morocco.
facts_added.source: Salem et al. 2025, Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-025-08793-7; Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology press release, April 2025

facts_added.fact: Nabta Playa's circle is about 4 m across with four sets of upright slabs as gates, giving sightlines roughly to the north and to the June solstice sunrise; a hearth beside it gave a radiocarbon date of 6,800 +/- 60 bp; the circle has been moved to the Nubian Museum in Aswan for protection.
facts_added.source: Malville 2015, Handbook of Archaeoastronomy and Ethnoastronomy, doi:10.1007/978-1-4614-6141-8_101

facts_added.fact: Nabta's excavators replied that the dates proposed for star alignments in the Orion map claims are about 1,500 years earlier than their best estimates for the construction of the megalithic structures, and that some megaliths may not stand where they were first set.
facts_added.source: Malville, Schild, Wendorf & Brenmer 2008, African Cultural Astronomy, doi:10.1007/978-1-4020-6639-9_11

facts_added.fact: Nabta Playa's region became uninhabitable about 4,800 radiocarbon years ago, and the authors suggest the exodus may have stimulated social complexity in predynastic Upper Egypt.
facts_added.source: Malville et al. 1998, Nature, doi:10.1038/33131

facts_added.fact: Lake Yoa (Ounianga, northern Chad) records a gradual, not abrupt, end of the humid period in the eastern Sahara: large-scale dust from about 4,300 years ago and today's desert ecosystem by about 2,700 years ago.
facts_added.source: Kropelin et al. 2008, Science, doi:10.1126/science.1154913

facts_added.fact: The end of the African Humid Period was locally abrupt but came progressively later at lower latitudes.
facts_added.source: Shanahan et al. 2015, Nature Geoscience, doi:10.1038/ngeo2329

facts_added.fact: A climate-vegetation model finds the Green Sahara most susceptible to collapse 7,000 to 6,000 years ago, at least 500 years before the observed collapse: pastoralism may have delayed the end; others argue grazing sped it up.
facts_added.source: Brierley, Manning & Maslin 2018, Nature Communications, doi:10.1038/s41467-018-06321-y; Wright 2017, Frontiers in Earth Science, doi:10.3389/feart.2017.00004

facts_added.fact: Radiocarbon dates from about 150 excavations in the eastern Sahara show settlement after the onset of humid conditions about 8500 BCE and an exodus with gradual drying from 5300 BCE; the authors argue the southward shift of the desert margin helped trigger pharaonic civilisation.
facts_added.source: Kuper & Kropelin 2006, Science, doi:10.1126/science.1130989

facts_added.fact: A primary pastoral community emerged in the Egyptian and Sudanese Nile Valley in the fifth millennium BC; its chronology challenges explanations that put climate stress first.
facts_added.source: Wengrow et al. 2014, Antiquity, doi:10.1017/S0003598X00050249

facts_added.fact: The Garamantes' oasis towns in Fazzan were the first towns of the central Sahara (trade, not farming alone, called them into being); hundreds of foggaras were used from about 400 BCE to 700 CE, and falling water tables and failing foggaras may have contributed to the decline.
facts_added.source: Mattingly & Sterry 2013, Antiquity, doi:10.1017/S0003598X00049097; Sterry, Mattingly & Wilson 2022, Oriental Institute Seminars 13

facts_added.fact: In 1958 Henri Lhote described one giant Round Head figure at Jabbaren as the 'great Martian god'; Le Quellec reads the name as a pleasantry, and ancient astronaut writers later took it literally.
facts_added.source: Le Quellec 2009, Des Martiens au Sahara: chroniques d'archeologie romantique, Actes Sud (new edition 2023, Editions du Detour)

facts_added.fact: As the eastern Sahara dried from about 5300 BCE, people were forced to the Nile valley or to ecological refuges, or south into the Sudanese Sahara; settlement lasted longer in the oases and favoured places such as Dakhla, the Nabta and Kiseiba region and the Gilf Kebir.
facts_added.source: Kuper & Kropelin 2006, Science, doi:10.1126/science.1130989; Bubenzer & Riemer 2007, Geoarchaeology, doi:10.1002/gea.20176

facts_added.fact: Nabta's own excavators note that the gaps in the circle's gates are a bit too wide, and the gates too close, for precise calendar measurements: the 'calendar circle' may be the wrong name.
facts_added.source: Wendorf & Malville 2001, in Holocene Settlement of the Egyptian Sahara, vol. 1: 489-502

facts_added.fact: Brophy proposed that stones inside the circle map Orion's belt, shoulders and head, with dates around 4800 BC and 6270 BC; the excavators reply that his dates are about 1,500 years earlier than the megaliths, whose C-line may not stand where it was set.
facts_added.source: Brophy & Rosen 2005, Mediterranean Archaeology and Archaeometry 5(1); Malville, Schild, Wendorf & Brenmer 2008, African Cultural Astronomy
